briefs.title: Active Funds Usually Lose the Long-Horizon Race
briefs.studyWindow: Long-horizon scorecards across rolling 5-, 10-, and 15-year periods
briefs.signal: Across major SPIVA scorecards, most active equity managers fail to beat their benchmark after costs over longer horizons.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: The durable pattern is not that active management never works. It is that persistence is weak, fees compound, and benchmark-relative underperformance dominates over long measurement windows.
briefs.mechanism: Active management is a zero-sum game before costs and a negative-sum game after fees, taxes, and trading friction.
briefs.whereItWorks: A low-cost indexed core is the strongest default for broad market exposure, retirement accounts, and investors who do not have a repeatable manager-selection process.
briefs.whereItBreaks: This does not imply every active strategy is worthless. Taxes, capacity, benchmark choice, and narrow mandates can change the comparison, but those are exceptions rather than the default case.
briefs.executionFriction: Low. The main friction is staying disciplined when an active narrative feels more compelling than a dull benchmark.
briefs.sourceName: S&P Dow Jones Indices SPIVA scorecards

briefs.title: Lump Sum Beats Dollar-Cost Averaging More Often Than Most Investors Expect
briefs.studyWindow: Historical market simulations across the United States, United Kingdom, and Australia
briefs.signal: When cash is available to invest, lump-sum deployment has historically beaten staged averaging in most observed windows because markets rise more often than they fall.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: The core tradeoff is simple. DCA reduces entry regret and short-term timing risk, but it also leaves capital unexposed for longer in an asset class with positive expected return.
briefs.mechanism: Expected equity returns are positive over time. Delaying exposure is a form of temporary de-risking, not a free lunch.
briefs.whereItWorks: Best as a default when the investor already has an adequate reserve and the cash is meant for long-term market exposure.
briefs.whereItBreaks: If the money is needed soon, if the investor is likely to abandon the plan after an early drawdown, or if the reserve stack is weak, DCA can be behaviorally safer.
briefs.executionFriction: Moderate. The friction is psychological, not mechanical.
briefs.sourceName: Vanguard research on cost averaging versus immediate investing

briefs.title: Emergency Fund Size Should Track Income Volatility, Not a Fixed Internet Rule
briefs.studyWindow: Recent U.S. household financial wellbeing surveys
briefs.signal: Household survey data continue to show that unexpected-expense fragility is common, which makes liquid reserves more than a comfort preference.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: A static three-month or six-month rule misses the real variable: income interruption risk. Households with unstable cash inflows, single-earner dependence, or high fixed costs need a wider reserve band than households with stable salaries and low burn.
briefs.mechanism: Cash reserves are insurance against forced selling, expensive debt use, and plan disruption during shocks.
briefs.whereItWorks: The reserve framework is strongest when tied to actual household burn, job volatility, and debt obligations rather than generic social-media targets.
briefs.whereItBreaks: Holding excessive cash becomes costly once the reserve size exceeds credible short-horizon risk and begins crowding out long-term investing.
briefs.executionFriction: Moderate. The friction is opportunity cost and the temptation to invest every idle dollar.
briefs.sourceName: Federal Reserve Survey of Household Economics and Decisionmaking

briefs.title: HYSA, Money Market Funds, and T-Bills Solve Different Problems
briefs.studyWindow: Current rate regime plus institutional cash-management mechanics
briefs.signal: The right cash vehicle is usually determined by liquidity timing and operational risk, not by chasing the last few basis points of yield.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: High-yield savings accounts maximize convenience, money market funds tend to track policy rates more closely, and short-term Treasuries can improve yield for known cash needs if maturity timing is acceptable.
briefs.mechanism: Each vehicle sits on a different point of the liquidity, settlement, and yield frontier.
briefs.whereItWorks: A layered stack works well: immediate cash in a bank account, core reserve in a money market or HYSA, and known future liabilities in short-term Treasuries.
briefs.whereItBreaks: Yield comparisons become misleading when the user ignores settlement delay, transfer friction, tax treatment, or the need for same-day liquidity.
briefs.executionFriction: Low to moderate. The main friction is account setup and transfer discipline.
briefs.sourceName: U.S. Treasury and cash-market product disclosures

briefs.title: Debt Avalanche Wins on Math, Snowball Can Win on Adherence
briefs.signal: Paying the highest-rate balance first minimizes interest cost, but behavioral evidence suggests many borrowers stick longer with methods that create quick visible wins.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: There is no real mathematical debate between avalanche and snowball. The live question is whether a lower-cost plan that fails is better than a slightly less efficient plan that survives long enough to clear the debt stack.
briefs.mechanism: Avalanche optimizes interest arithmetic. Snowball exploits reinforcement and attention management.
briefs.whereItWorks: Avalanche is the correct default for borrowers with good system discipline, autopay, and enough bandwidth to stay on plan.
briefs.whereItBreaks: Snowball may be the better protocol for borrowers with chronic restart risk, scattered balances, or stress-driven avoidance behavior.
briefs.executionFriction: Moderate. The friction is mostly behavioral and administrative rather than analytical.
briefs.sourceName: Philip B. Shane on credit-card debt payment patterns

briefs.title: Asset Location Can Raise After-Tax Return Without Taking More Market Risk
briefs.signal: Placing tax-inefficient assets in tax-advantaged accounts and tax-efficient assets in taxable accounts can improve after-tax compounding without changing headline allocation.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: The magnitude varies with tax bracket, account mix, turnover, and future withdrawal rates, but the direction is usually favorable when a household has multiple account wrappers to work with.
briefs.mechanism: The strategy works by shielding high-distribution or ordinary-income-heavy assets from current taxation while preserving tax-efficient growth in taxable accounts.
briefs.whereItWorks: Best for households with taxable brokerage, tax-deferred accounts, and Roth capacity all active at once.
briefs.whereItBreaks: It matters less for small balances, simple two-fund portfolios, low tax brackets, or investors whose future tax regime is likely to reverse the benefit.
briefs.executionFriction: Moderate. Rebalancing, withdrawal planning, and account-level constraints make implementation less trivial than the theory suggests.
briefs.sourceName: Vanguard and similar after-tax portfolio research

briefs.title: Roth Conversions Are a Tax-Rate Bet, Not a Universal Upgrade
briefs.studyWindow: Current IRS rules with forward-looking tax-rate scenarios
briefs.signal: A Roth conversion can be attractive when current marginal tax cost is low relative to expected future withdrawal tax cost, but the case weakens quickly when the tax paid today is too high.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: The strategy is not inherently good or bad. It depends on current bracket, future spending path, available outside cash to pay the tax, legacy goals, and interaction with Medicare premiums or Social Security taxation.
briefs.mechanism: The investor prepays tax at today’s rate in exchange for future tax-free qualified withdrawals and reduced tax-deferred account drag.
briefs.whereItWorks: Strongest in low-income bridge years, before required distributions, and when the tax can be paid from external cash rather than the converted assets.
briefs.whereItBreaks: Weak when current taxable income is already high, the conversion pushes the household into expensive cliffs, or future withdrawals were likely to occur at lower effective rates.
briefs.executionFriction: High. Timing, bracket control, and downstream interactions make this strategy easy to mis-execute.
briefs.sourceName: IRS IRA guidance and retirement tax-planning literature

briefs.title: Automatic Enrollment Changes Retirement Saving More Reliably Than Motivation Alone
briefs.signal: Default effects in retirement plans consistently raise participation relative to opt-in systems, especially for workers who would otherwise delay or never start.
briefs.empiricalBaseline: The strongest savings interventions are often structural rather than motivational. Defaults, automatic escalation, and payroll deduction outperform willpower-driven monthly saving plans on adherence.
briefs.mechanism: People tend to stick with defaults. Automation removes repeated choice points and reduces behavioral leakage.
briefs.whereItWorks: Most effective in employer plans with automatic enrollment, gradual contribution escalation, and broad low-cost default investment options.
briefs.whereItBreaks: Defaults can still be too low, and some workers anchor to the default instead of saving at a level that fits their actual retirement burden.
briefs.executionFriction: Low. Once in place, the system mostly runs itself.
briefs.sourceName: Madrian and Shea on the power of suggestion in 401(k) participation
